Note that, even if you do not know that Kobasa's concept of hardiness is also known as psychological hardiness, you would want to choose answer A because, of the answers given, it comes closest to what you know.
In contrast to the commonly held belief that women experience greater work-family conflict than men do, the Shockley et al. meta-analysis found that men and women report similar levels of conflict.
According to Maslach and colleagues (2001), resistance is not one of the core characteristics of job burnout.

Cohen-Charash and Spector's (2001) meta-analysis of research on the effects of organizational justice found that job satisfaction is positively and similarly related to perceived procedural, distributive, and interactional justice.
Faragher, Cass, and Cooper's (2005) meta-analysis found that job satisfaction is related to both mental and physical health, with the relationship being stronger for mental health.

in_book.content: To alleviate the low motivation of her employees, the employer familiar with Vroom's expectancy theory would ask them about everything except commitment.

To increase motivation and satisfaction of employees at Best Plumbing Supply, the organizational psychologist will most likely recommend that the owner redesign the employees' jobs to provide opportunities for autonomy, responsibility, and advancement, as this is consistent with Herzberg's (1966) two-factor theory.
The five core job dimensions identified by the job characteristics model are skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and feedback.

Equity theory predicts that a worker's motivation is affected by the comparisons the worker makes between their input/outcome ratio and the input/outcome ratios of workers doing the same or a similar job.
Maslow's need hierarchy theory predicts that, when a person's physiological and safety needs have been satisfied, the person will be motivated primarily by their social needs.

When interviewing employees to determine how to alleviate low motivation, an employer familiar with equity theory will focus on the employees' perceptions of the relative fairness of their treatment at work.
Herzberg's two-factor theory predicts that job enrichment is the best way to increase employees' job motivation and satisfaction.
Equity theory predicts that a worker's motivation is affected by the worker's perceptions of the degree to which he/she is being treated fairly compared to other workers.

According to expectancy theory, an employee's motivation is determined by their beliefs about the likelihood that exerting effort on-the-job will result in successful job performance, the belief that successful performance will result in certain outcomes, and the value of those outcomes.
According to expectancy theory, the belief that is most negatively affected in the situation where Jill Doe did not receive the promised raises despite excellent job evaluations is instrumentality.

Hackman and Oldham's (1980) job characteristics model predicts that designing a job so it provides employees with five core job characteristics will have the greatest positive impact on employees who are high in growth-need strength.
In the context of expectancy theory, expectancy refers to an employee's belief that adequate effort will lead to successful performance.

proprietary.content: Research on goal-setting theory has found that, when supervisees participate in setting their own performance goals, the goals tend to be more difficult than the goals the supervisor would have set alone.
A supervisee's participation in setting goals is not always necessary for his/her commitment to goals but is important when a supervisee is not likely to accept assigned goals.
People with a high need for achievement are not motivated most by opportunities for gaining status and recognition.

in_book.content: Behavior modeling is based on Bandura's (1986) social cognitive theory of learning and involves having trainees observe a model perform the desired behaviors and giving trainees feedback and reinforcement while they practice modeled behaviors.
Kirkpatrick's evaluation model for training programs identifies results as the most informative level, followed by behavior, learning, and reaction.
According to Kirkpatrick's (1998) evaluation model, reaction criteria provide the least valuable information about the effects of a training program.

proprietary.content: The developer of a training program conducts a summative evaluation immediately after the program has been delivered to assess trainee reactions and the program's effectiveness.
Providing "identical elements" is most important for ensuring transfer of training when designing a training program.
Vestibule training is chosen as the optimal method of training because it is less dangerous than on-the-job training.
A needs analysis is conducted to identify training needs and often includes an organizational analysis, task analysis, person analysis, and demographic analysis.
Cross-training is a method used to teach each member of a team the essential tasks performed by other team members.

A formative evaluation is conducted during the development of a training program to determine what changes need to be made for the program to achieve its goals, and it may include having experts review the content of each component of the program and administering measures of attitudes and learning to trainees following delivery of each component.
An organizational psychologist will conduct a needs analysis to determine if the performance of many of its recently hired employees can be improved by providing them with training.
Overlearning involves continuing to practice newly acquired skills beyond the point of mastery, resulting in automaticity.

Overlearning is most useful for skills and knowledge that will be used infrequently on-the-job, as it results in automaticity, which is especially important for tasks performed relatively infrequently and when correct performance is essential because errors can have serious negative consequences.
When acquiring new knowledge or a new skill, overlearning is particularly important when performance errors are likely to be costly.
Summative evaluation, as described by Trochim (2020), does not include implementation evaluation.
The least accurate description of mentoring in organizations is that mentors identify the agenda for the nature and goals of their relationships with mentees.

in_book.content: Proactive interference occurs when prior learning (e.g., Spanish) interferes with the ability to learn or recall new information (e.g., French), as illustrated by Ella's experience.
The keyword method is particularly useful for foreign (second) language learning.
Tolman and Honzik concluded that rats allowed to explore a maze without being given a reward formed cognitive maps of the maze, confirming that latent learning occurs without reinforcement.
Prospective memory refers to memory for tasks that must be performed or events that will occur in the future, such as remembering that you have a dentist appointment next Thursday morning.

Miller's (1956) "magical number seven, plus or minus two" refers to the capacity of short-term memory, which Miller found to be limited to between five and nine (seven plus and minus two) chunks of information.
Sensory memory has a large capacity and brief duration, storing information directly from the environment for about one-quarter second to four seconds.
Bandura's (1986) social cognitive theory attributes the acquisition of many complex behaviors to observing the behavior of others.
The method of loci, which involves visually placing each item in a list of unrelated words in different locations in a familiar place, is most useful for remembering such a list.
Baddeley's multi-component model of working memory identifies the episodic buffer as responsible for integrating new verbal and visual information.
The episodic buffer is a component of working memory, as described by Baddeley (2000).
Episodic and semantic memory are types of declarative memory.

Retroactive interference, where more recently acquired information interferes with the ability to recall previously learned information, explains why you called your co-worker's husband "Bob" after earlier meeting him as "Bill".
Without rehearsal, information remains in short-term memory for about 20 to 30 seconds.

The research by Jenkins and Dallenbach (1924) found that people who slept after learning new information recalled the information better than those who stayed awake for the same length of time after learning the information and engaged in an unrelated activity, contradicting the predictions of trace decay theory.

According to the encoding specificity hypothesis, forgetting is caused by inadequate retrieval cues, where conditions at the time of recall are not the same as the conditions at the time of encoding new information.
The use of the phrase "on old Olympus towering top, a Finn and German viewed some hops" by a psychology student is an example of an acrostic technique to remember the 12 cranial nerves.
In Baddeley's (2000) multi-component model of working memory, the episodic buffer is responsible for integrating information in working memory with information in long-term memory.

Subjects in a memory experiment are asked to recite the alphabet two times after memorizing a list of words in order to prevent rehearsal of the list, which can be used to assess the effects of retroactive interference.
In the method of loci, each word in a list is visually linked to a familiar site or object to help encode and recall the list of unrelated words.
Elaborative rehearsal is considered the most effective way to transfer new information from short- to long-term memory.
Baddeley's (2000) multi-component model describes working memory as consisting of a central executive and three subsystems, which do not include a semantic register.
The primacy effect in the serial position effect is due to the transfer of information from short- to long-term memory.
Research suggests that the mediator effectiveness hypothesis is most useful for understanding the "testing effect."
Retroactive interference occurs when recently learned information interferes with the ability to recall previously learned information.
As described by Baddeley (2000), the phonological loop temporarily stores auditory information.

Priming is a method for studying implicit memory, and there are several types of priming, including repetition priming, which occurs when presentation of a word or object facilitates later identification of that word or object in a different format or context, and word-stem completion and word-fragment completion are two of the repetition priming tasks that are used to investigate implicit memory.
Tolman's research with rats confirmed that learning can occur without being apparent in behavior.

Subjects in a research study who read a list of semantically related words and then recalled "anger" as one of the words, even though it was not included in the list, illustrate the phenomenon of illusory memory or false memory.

Retrieval from long-term memory is maximized when the conditions at the time of learning (encoding) new information are the same as the conditions when the information must be recalled, as described by the encoding specificity hypothesis.

proprietary.content: Wolfgang Kohler concluded that deriving a solution to a problem can be the result of insight, which involves mentally restructuring the elements of the problem in order to see it in a new way.

When research participants are asked to memorize a list of unrelated words and then recall the words in any order after a brief delay, they will recall words from the beginning of the list better than words from the middle or end of the list, due to the serial position effect.

in_book.content: This man's symptoms are characteristic of contralateral neglect, which is caused by damage to the parietal lobe (most often the right parietal lobe), and a person with this disorder is unaware of areas and objects on the side of his/her body opposite to the location of the damage.
Damage to Broca's area produces nonfluent speech with intact comprehension.
Anosognosia is most commonly caused by damage to the right parietal lobe and is characterized by a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability.

A split-brain patient will be able to say "knife" when the picture of a knife is projected to the right visual field, and although the patient can't say "fork," the patient will be able to pick out a fork with the left hand when the picture of a fork is briefly presented to the left visual field.
Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize familiar faces.
Lesions in the dorsolateral area of the prefrontal cortex are most likely to cause deficits in insight, planning, judgment, and other executive functions.
Sperry and Gazzaniga's (1967) "split-brain patients" had their corpus callosums severed as a treatment for severe epileptic seizures.

Damage to certain areas of the dominant parietal lobe can produce Gerstmann's syndrome, which involves four symptoms: finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia (difficulty writing), and acalculia (difficulty performing simple mathematical operations), but not ataxia (loss of muscle control), which is usually caused by damage to the cerebellum.
Individuals with Wernicke's aphasia have impaired comprehension of spoken and written language and fluent speech that's devoid of meaning.
Conduction aphasia, which is usually caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus, is characterized by fluent spontaneous speech, normal comprehension, and impaired repetition.
Ideomotor apraxia is usually caused by damage to the left (dominant) parietal lobe.
Damage to the frontal lobe causes perseveration, which involves repetition of the same response or action when it's inappropriate to do so in a variety of situations and on a variety of tasks.

A split-brain patient presented with the word "COPYCAT" will say "CAT" and point to "COPY" with their left hand, as the left visual field and right hemisphere cannot communicate with the right visual field and left hemisphere.
The dichotic listening task is used to obtain information about hemispheric specialization.
Lesions in the parietal lobe cause the condition of tactile agnosia, in which a person is unable to recognize familiar objects by touch following a closed head injury.
Right hemisphere damage is associated with impairments in both emotional prosody and pragmatics.
Left-hemisphere dominance for language is found in about 95% of right-handed people and 70% of left-handed people.

Following a stroke that caused left-sided hemiplegia, a woman exhibiting asomatognosia, which is a lack of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, often involving the left hemiplegic arm and accompanied by anosognosia, a lack of awareness or denial of one's illness, due to damage to certain areas of the right parietal lobe.
Conduction aphasia is characterized by relatively intact comprehension, fluent aphasia, anomia, and impaired repetition, and is caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus.
Damage to the left parietal lobe can result in ideomotor apraxia, an inability to perform purposeful motor movements when asked to do so.
Carl's symptoms of contralateral neglect, including bumping into things on the left side and drawing only the right side of a house, indicate an injury to his parietal lobe.

Damage to the orbitofrontal region of the prefrontal cortex is most suggestive of the symptoms exhibited by a 48-year-old man with a traumatic brain injury, including emotion dysregulation, immature behavior, impulsivity, and lack of empathy.

Frontal lobe damage often has an adverse effect on motivation, judgment, and memory but not on IQ test scores, as frontal lobe damage seems to have a negative impact on divergent thinking but not on convergent thinking which is what is measured by standard IQ tests.
Conduction aphasia involves fluent (but paraphasic) speech, relatively intact comprehension, poor word repetition, and impaired naming.
A 74-year-old woman experiences complete paralysis on the right side of her body, which is referred to as hemiplegia and is due to damage in the left side of her brain.
Symptoms of frontal lobe injury are most likely to include an inability to interact spontaneously with others, fluctuations in mood, and difficulty planning a complex sequence of movements.

People with limb-kinetic apraxia would have the most trouble picking up a paper clip or small coin from a table, as this type of apraxia involves an inability to make precise, coordinated movements with fingers, hands, arms, or legs.
The consolidation of emotional memories is mediated primarily by the amygdala.

The cerebellum is the brain area most likely affected by the skateboarding accident that caused Cody, a 17-year-old, to exhibit symptoms like clumsiness, slurred speech, and other symptoms associated with alcohol intoxication.
The thalamus processes and transfers all incoming sensory information except olfactory information to appropriate areas in the cerebral cortex.

The hippocampus is involved in consolidating long-term declarative memories, and its injury would likely result in the inability to form new long-term declarative memories, as seen in the young woman with a traumatic brain injury.
Electrical stimulation of a person's ascending reticular activating system will wake up a sleeping person and cause an awake person to become more alert.

Kluver and Bucy (1938) found that bilateral lesioning of the amygdala, hippocampus, and temporal lobes in rhesus monkeys caused visual agnosia, reduced fear, increased docility, dietary changes, and abnormal sexual behavior.
The hypothalamus helps maintain the body's homeostasis by regulating body temperature, fluid and electrolyte balance, blood pressure, and other important functions.

The basal ganglia are involved in the regulation of voluntary movement and consist of the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus, and a number of disorders have been linked to abnormalities in these structures including Tourette's disorder, ADHD, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Various areas of the hypothalamus have been linked to different types of aggressive behavior in several animal species, with electrical stimulation of the medial hypothalamus usually producing affective attack behavior and electrical stimulation of the lateral hypothalamus producing stalking attack behavior in cats and other animal species.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus controls the sleep-wake cycle by triggering changes in the release of melatonin by the pineal gland.
People with bilateral damage to the amygdala often have difficulty recognizing negative emotions in facial expressions, especially fear.
Areas of the cerebral cortex involved in the planning and execution of movement send excitatory signals to the striatum.
Stress-induced increases in cortisol levels in the hippocampus have been linked to impairments in the retrieval of declarative memories.
The amnesia associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is due to damage to the thalamus and mammillary bodies.
An overdose of morphine, heroin, or other opioid can cause respiratory failure because of its effects on the medulla oblongata, which controls respiration and other vital autonomic functions.
Oxytocin is a hormone produced by the hypothalamus that is important for stimulating milk ejection during breastfeeding.
Increasing the level of oxytocin in healthy adults who do not have deficits in emotion perception can cause them to become overly sensitive to the emotional facial expressions of others.
Electrical stimulation of certain areas of the amygdala elicits responses associated with conditioned fear such as freezing, increased heart rate and blood pressure, and release of stress hormones.
Opioid-induced respiratory depression is due to the effects of opiates on receptors in the medulla.

Neuroimaging studies have linked posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) to a reduced volume of the hippocampus, decreased activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and increased activity in the amygdala.

The suprachiasmatic nucleus located in the hypothalamus controls the body's circadian rhythms (24-hour cycles), which include the sleep-wake cycle and daily changes in core body temperature and the secretion of several hormones.
The medulla oblongata is part of the hindbrain, and damage can result in death because it regulates a number of vital life functions.
Sam's inability to remove the cork from the wine bottle despite knowing the goal is an example of apraxia.
Intravenous administration of vitamin B1 (thiamine) is the primary treatment for Wernicke's encephalopathy.

Neurocognitive disorder caused by prion disease is not potentially reversible.

The Coloured Progressive Matrices is a version of Raven's Progressive Matrices for children ages 5 to 11, older adults, and individuals with mental or physical impairments that assesses nonverbal intelligence.

proprietary.content: The Columbia Mental Maturity Scale is useful for assessing children 3 to 10 years of age who have sensory, motor, or speech deficits and was originally developed for children with cerebral palsy.
An advantage of computerized adaptive tests is that they reduce testing time without losing precision of measurement.

in_book.content: The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) was developed based on Murray's personality theory, which describes personality as the result of internal and external forces, such as biological and psychological needs and environmental pressures.

Confabulation on the Rorschach, which involves overgeneralizing from one detail of an inkblot to the whole inkblot, is associated with a thought disorder caused by organic brain injury or a functional disorder.
The items included in the EPPS (Edwards Personal Preference Schedule) assess the 15 needs identified in Murray's theory of needs (e.g., achievement, autonomy, affiliation, dominance).
The purpose of the inquiry phase in administering the Rorschach is to obtain the information needed to accurately code the examinee's responses.
Evidence for the five-factor model of personality has been provided by lexical research, which is based on the assumption that universally important personality traits are encoded in language.

For the clinical diagnosis of personality disorders, self-report measures are most useful as initial screening devices that are followed by a semistructured interview when they indicate a client has symptoms of a personality disorder.
The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is based on Jung's personality typology and provides information on four bipolar personality dimensions.
The development of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator was based on Jung's theory of psychological types and the personality research of Isabel Briggs Myers and Katherine Cook Briggs.

Form quality is a measure of perceptual accuracy and indicates the extent to which the examinee's response corresponds to the actual shape of the inkblot when scoring and interpreting the Rorschach test.

proprietary.content: The NEO-PI-3 (NEO Personality Inventory-3) provides scores on the five major domains of personality: neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness to experience.

The Leiter International Performance Scale, Third Edition (Leiter-3) is a measure of cognitive abilities for individuals ages 3 to 75+ that is useful for non-English speakers and individuals with language impairments.
Research on the Fagan Test of Intelligence has confirmed that selective attention to novel stimuli in infancy is a good predictor of IQ in childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood.
Cattell used the lexical method and factor analysis to develop the Sixteen Personality Factor (16PF) Questionnaire.

A meta-analysis found that both self- and informant-ratings of individuals with Alzheimer's disease indicated significantly higher levels of neuroticism and lower levels of openness and extraversion compared to those without the disease.

in_book.content: The Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5) provides four types of composite scores, including Factor Index scores, that have a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.
Individuals with mild Alzheimer's disease typically obtain the highest scores on the Verbal Comprehension Index and the lowest scores on the Processing Speed Index of the WAIS-IV.

The SB5 is based on the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model of cognitive abilities and provides scores on five factors derived from that model: knowledge, fluid reasoning, quantitative reasoning, visual-spatial processing, and working memory.
A 20-year-old who has received a diagnosis of ADHD would likely obtain the highest score on the Verbal Comprehension index of the WAIS-IV.
The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition (WISC-V) is appropriate for individuals ages 6.0 to 16.11.
The WAIS-IV full-scale and index scores have a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15, and the individual subtests have a mean of 10 and standard deviation of 3.
The WAIS-IV General Ability Index (GAI) score is useful for obtaining a measure of intelligence that minimizes the effects of working memory and processing speed.
Adults with traumatic brain injury are most likely to obtain the highest score on the Verbal Comprehension Index of the WAIS-IV.

The Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5) provides scores on the following five cognitive factors: Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing, and Working Memory, but not Abstract Reasoning.
The WPPSI-IV (Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, 4th Edition) is appropriate for examinees ages 2:6 to 7:7.
Children with ADHD included in the WISC-V standardization sample obtained the lowest score on the Processing Speed Index.
The SB5 intelligence test is appropriate for a 12-year-old child, with an age range of 2:0 to 85+ years, unlike the WPPSI-IV, WAIS-IV, and CMMS which have different age ranges.
The WAIS-IV Processing Speed Index consists of the Symbol Search and Coding subtests, and the supplemental Cancellation subtest.

The WAIS-IV's Global Ability Index (GAI) is based on Verbal Comprehension and Perceptual Reasoning subtest scores, and it's useful when an examiner wants to obtain a measure of general intelligence that's not affected by processing speed or working memory.
Individuals with nonverbal learning disability (NVLD) tend to obtain significantly higher scores on the WAIS-IV's Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI) than on the Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI).
The Technical and Interpretive Manual for the WAIS-IV reports the results of several factor analyses that support the test's underlying four-factor structure.

The "classic aging pattern" on measures of IQ refers to the tendency of scores on verbal tests (crystallized intelligence) to hold up fairly well with increasing age while scores on performance tests (fluid intelligence) begin to decline in the 20s.

proprietary.content: Age-related changes in fluid intelligence have been linked to changes in processing speed and working memory.

In the context of psychological assessment, the terms "floor" and "ceiling" refer to the degree to which a test can discriminate among examinees who have very low levels or very high levels of the characteristic measured by the test, with a limited floor indicating the test cannot discriminate well among examinees with low levels, and a limited ceiling indicating the test cannot discriminate well among examinees with high levels.
The SB5 administration begins with two routing subtests: object series/matrices and vocabulary.
Fluid intelligence begins to decline at about 30 to 40 years of age, while crystallized intelligence continues to increase and peaks at 60 to 70 years of age.
A measure of fluid intelligence would not include items that assess numerical reasoning.

Providing adults with training on a demanding working memory task is likely to improve their fluid intelligence even when the working memory task is not similar in format to the fluid intelligence task.
Brain activity in the caudate nucleus is elevated in people with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and cognitive behavior therapy has been shown to reduce that activity.
Exposure with response prevention is a research-supported treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Interoceptive exposure is a technique used in the treatment of panic disorder that involves exposing the individual to the physical sensations associated with a panic attack.

In vivo exposure and response prevention is considered the first-line treatment for agoraphobia, and the research has found that combining exposure with applied relaxation, breathing retraining, or cognitive techniques does not significantly improve outcomes.
For generalized anxiety disorder, the combination of motivational interviewing and CBT is more effective than CBT alone for reducing worry, especially when initial worry is severe.
In vivo exposure is most effective when it's paired with applied tension rather than relaxation for specific phobia, blood-injection-injury type.

Research has consistently found internet-delivered cognitive behavior therapy (iCBT) to be equivalent to in-person CBT for reducing the symptoms of social anxiety disorder, with studies also confirming that the beneficial effects of iCBT are short- and long-term.

in_book.content: Successful treatment with cognitive behavior therapy for a specific phobia will most likely lead to decreased activity in the amygdala, insula, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and increased activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, according to functional neuroimaging findings.

proprietary.content: Cognitive-behavioral therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy are evidence-based treatments for postpartum depression, especially postpartum depression with mild to moderate symptoms.

Family-focused therapy is the treatment-of-choice for a 16-year-old with bipolar I disorder when their parents have become increasingly overprotective and emotionally overinvolved, increasing conflicts between them and the child.

Parent-child interaction therapy (PCIT) is an evidence-based family treatment for young children with conduct disorder or other disruptive behavior disorder, and has also been found to be effective for children with a history of maltreatment.
Multisystemic therapy is about equally effective for African American youth and European youth.
The treatment-of-choice for a 6-year-old child with oppositional defiant disorder who has been physically abused by their parents is parent-child interaction therapy.
Family-based treatment for bulimia (FB-BN) involves greater collaboration between parents and the affected adolescent compared to family-based treatment for anorexia (FB-AN).
Cognitive-behavioral therapy and interpersonal psychotherapy are evidence-based treatments for binge-eating disorder.

in_book.content: Research has confirmed that the night alarm, also known as the moisture alarm, enuresis alarm, and bell-and-pad, has the best long-term effects for children who have received a DSM-5 diagnosis of enuresis, nocturnal only.

proprietary.content: The moisture alarm has the best long-term effects as the most effective treatment for a child's nocturnal enuresis that is not due to a medical condition.

Family-based treatment for adolescents with anorexia nervosa takes an agnostic view of the disorder and consists of three phases: parental control of the adolescent's eating, gradual return of control to the adolescent, and establishing age-appropriate independence in the adolescent.
Regulated breathing has been found to be an effective treatment for childhood-onset fluency disorder, also known as stuttering.
Lovaas (1987) used discrimination training and shaping to teach young nonspeaking children with autism spectrum disorder to communicate verbally.
Evidence-based parent-training in behavior management (PTBM) is considered the first-line treatment for preschool children 4 and 5 years of age with ADHD.

in_book.content: When a therapist is using dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) with a client who has recently received the diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, the client's treatment will least likely include family or couple counseling.

proprietary.content: Dialectical behavior therapy is based on the assumption that borderline personality disorder is a disorder of the emotion regulation system that involves high emotional vulnerability coupled with an inability to regulate emotions.

The primary goals of individual therapy in dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) are to reduce quality-of-life interfering behaviors and therapy-interfering behaviors, and to eliminate life-threatening behaviors, except for self-triggering behaviors.

Practitioners of dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) primarily aim to increase generalization of behavioral skills acquired during therapy to everyday situations and crises, as well as repair the therapeutic relationship.

in_book.content: Orgasmic reconditioning has been identified as an effective treatment for paraphilic disorder.

Interventions for genito-pelvic pain disorder include relaxation training, sensate focus, a topical anesthetic, vaginal dilators, and Kegel exercises, but orgasmic reconditioning is used to treat paraphilic disorders.

proprietary.content: The squeeze and start/stop techniques are the two most commonly used behavioral interventions for premature ejaculation.

Behavioral and cognitive-behavioral techniques have been found effective for treating female orgasmic disorder (FOD), and directed masturbation is the most empirically supported technique (especially for lifelong FOD) and is considered to be the first-line treatment for this disorder.

in_book.content: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention (RP) model proposes that high-risk situations are the immediate precipitants of alcohol use after a period of abstinence.

Community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT) is an evidence-based intervention that was designed for families that include an adult who has a substance use problem but refuses to seek treatment.

Community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT) does not involve helping the concerned significant other (CSO) adopt "loving-detachment" from the identified patient (IP) with the substance-use problem, as that is characteristic of Al-Anon.

Voucher-based reinforcement therapy (VBRT) is most effective for promoting initial abstinence, while cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) is most effective for preventing relapse in patients with cocaine use disorder.

proprietary.content: When using personalized normative feedback (PNF) as an intervention for Jacob, a 21-year-old college student who frequently engages in heavy alcohol use, his therapist will provide Jacob with information that allows him to compare the frequency of his drinking to the actual average frequency of drinking of other college students.

Project MATCH found that the three treatments (motivational enhancement therapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and twelve-step facilitation) produced similar reductions in drinking with a small advantage for twelve-step facilitation, and some support for the hypothesis that matching type of treatment to certain patient characteristics improves treatment outcomes.
Research has found that single-session psychological debriefing as a treatment for PTSD has not been effective and may actually increase PTSD symptoms.
Trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy (TF-CBT) is an evidence-based treatment that was initially designed for children and adolescents ages 3 to 18 years who have experienced sexual abuse.
Face-to-face therapy is similarly effective as computer videoconferencing therapy for reducing PTSD symptoms and for maintaining treatment fidelity.
In a normal distribution of scores, a T-score of 60 is equivalent to a z-score of 1.0 and a percentile rank of 84.
In a normal distribution, a percentile rank of 84 indicates that an examinee's score is one standard deviation above the mean.
A T-score distribution has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10.
In a normal distribution of scores with a mean of 75 and standard deviation of 5, a raw score of 65 is equivalent to a z-score of -2.0.
When raw scores are converted to percentile ranks, the resulting distribution will be rectangular.
In a normal distribution, a T-score of 40 is equivalent to a percentile rank of 16.
Percentage scores are a type of criterion-referenced score, while all other scores mentioned (e.g., z-scores, T-scores, percentile ranks) are norm-referenced scores.
In a normal distribution, a T-score of 40 represents the lowest score.

Percentile rank distributions are always flat regardless of the shape of the raw score distribution because percentile ranks are evenly distributed throughout the range of scores: The same number of scores fall between the percentile ranks of 1 and 10, 11 and 20, 21 and 30, etc.
In a normal distribution, a T-score of 65 represents the highest score.
Banding is based on the assumption that small differences in selection test scores are not necessarily associated with meaningful differences in job performance.
In a normal distribution, a percentile rank of 84 and a T-score of 60 are both one standard deviation above the mean.

in_book.content: The APA Ethics Code and Canadian Code of Ethics encourage pro bono services, as addressed in their General Principles.
A psychologist should provide requested confidential information about a former client to an Ethics Committee only after confirming the client has signed an authorization to release the information.

To be consistent with ethical requirements, a psychologist who specializes in treating depression but has not worked with African American or low-income clients should agree to see a new client from those populations as long as they consult with a colleague who has experience working with those clients.

Dr. Liu, a licensed psychologist, should provide emergency mental health services to the nearby rural community devastated by a flood until the emergency ends or alternative services become available, despite lacking specific experience working with victims of natural disasters.

The graduate student should discuss the ethical violation with the psychologist, as the psychologist's requirement that his students participate in the research without providing an alternative assignment violates ethical standards.
The APA Ethics Code states that APA may take action against a member who has been expelled or suspended from an affiliated state psychological association or convicted of a felony.

Dr. Andersen should consult with a colleague to help her monitor her effectiveness with clients and determine the best course of action, as she has realized that she hates going home after work and has started feeling negatively toward therapy clients who resemble her abrasive, alcoholic father-in-law.

To be consistent with ethical requirements, a psychodynamic psychotherapist with limited experience in mindfulness meditation should inform the client of their limited experience, discuss the client's options, and refer the client to a qualified therapist if they continue to want training in mindfulness meditation.

Denying a psychologist a promotion based solely on a pending ethics complaint against them would be unacceptable, as it violates ethical standards that require due process and natural justice procedures for employment decisions.
Hiring psychology graduate students to administer measures is acceptable as long as the students are provided with training in administering the measures and relevant ethical guidelines.

This situation is addressed in Standards 1.04 and 1.05 of the APA's Ethics Code and Standards II.43 and II.44 of the Canadian Code of Ethics, and an attempt at an informal resolution would be the best initial course of action.
As an ethical psychologist, Dr. Berstein should obtain professional consultation to determine the best course of action regarding her attraction to her client Rusty R.

A psychologist's new clients are a married couple and their two sons, ages 11 and 16, who moved to the United States from Mexico five years ago, and the psychologist, who does not speak Spanish, should not have the son or aunt act as an interpreter to avoid conflicts and inaccuracies due to a lack of objectivity.
As an ethical psychologist, Dr. Swenson should see the clients in therapy but seek consultation with a colleague who has relevant experience.

The best course of action when overhearing two members of the clerical staff complaining about the possible unethical behavior of a licensed psychologist, assuming client confidentiality is not an issue and you are not legally required to report the behavior, is to discuss the possible ethical violation with the psychologist.

A licensed psychologist, Dr. Ballard, should agree to see an adult client from an unfamiliar ethnic background and seek supervision or consultation by telephone, videoconference, or other means with someone who has experience working with members of this population.

Dr. Unger, a cognitive behavioral psychologist, may conduct therapy via telephone for a client with a disorder that has been successfully treated face-to-face if he has received adequate training in telepsychology, despite the lack of empirical evidence on its effectiveness when conducted via telephone.

Psychologists may prioritize ethical responsibilities or legal requirements, depending on the nature of the situation, when facing unresolvable conflicts between their ethical responsibilities and legal requirements, according to the ethics codes of the American and Canadian Psychological Associations.

To be consistent with ethical requirements, Dr. Linden should inform Raymond R. of her lack of experience with meditation, discuss his options with him, and give him a referral if he continues to want training in meditation.

Dr. Wallace should refer the family to a therapist who speaks Croatian but, if that's not possible, obtain the assistance of a professional interpreter, as the oldest daughter should not act as an interpreter to be consistent with ethical requirements.
Psychologists may not deny tenure or promotion to an employee solely because that employee is the complainant or respondent in a pending ethics complaint.

To be consistent with ethical requirements, Dr. Maddox should see older adults in therapy if she's able to obtain consultation while doing so with a colleague who has experience working with members of this population.
As an ethical psychologist, you should explain to Anita the seriousness of her allegation and discuss the options she has in the situation where another therapist touched her inappropriately.
When psychologists are faced with conflicts between ethical responsibilities and legal requirements, they may comply with legal requirements when doing so doesn't violate basic human rights.

Open access is most consistent with the General Principle of Justice in the APA's Ethics Code, which calls for fairness and justice to entitle all persons to access to and benefit from the contributions of psychology.
A psychologist should provide the Ethics Committee with the requested client information after confirming that the client has signed an authorization to release the information.

Accepting a small gift from a client to avoid causing them to "lose face" is most consistent with the APA Ethics Code principles of Beneficence/Nonmaleficence and Respect for People's Rights and Dignity.
Privilege is a legal concept that protects a client's confidential information from being disclosed in legal proceedings.

The potential limits of confidentiality should ordinarily be discussed with a therapy client at the outset of therapy and subsequently as needed, to be consistent with the requirements of the APA Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
The co-worker's sexually suggestive comments would represent sexual harassment if the co-worker does not stop making them after being told they're offensive, as per the APA Ethics Code.

Giving a client the business card of the psychologist's husband, who is a licensed massage therapist, is unacceptable because it violates ethical prohibitions against engaging in situations that create a conflict of interest.

Dr. Wilson, the court-hired psychologist evaluating the mental competence of a man charged as an accomplice in a bank robbery that ended in the death of a bank employee, provided the court only with information relevant to the man's mental competence, consistent with ethical requirements.
The holder of the privilege is ordinarily the client or the client's legal representative.

Consultation with colleagues is addressed in Standard 4.06 of the Ethics Code, which states that psychologists should not disclose confidential client information unless they have obtained the client's authorization or they do not disclose information "that reasonably could lead to the identification" of the client.
Quid pro quo sexual harassment involves a demand for sexual favors in exchange for job benefits.

After a person's death, the legally authorized person to whom psychologists can disclose confidential information with the appropriate consent is ordinarily the executor of the person's estate, the estate administrator, or other legal representative.
To fulfill ethical requirements for a research study involving 50 sixth grade students, the researcher should obtain assent from each student and permission from the parent(s) of each student.
Dr. Bright violated ethical requirements because changing the names of the family members was not adequate given that they are prominent citizens residing in a small town.

It is acceptable for a psychologist to decide not to continue seeing a client with antisocial personality disorder as long as the psychologist provides the client with referrals to other mental health professionals.

Dr. Miller, who has been hired by the court to conduct a court-ordered evaluation of Edward E., a defendant in a criminal case, does not have to obtain informed consent from Ed before proceeding with the evaluation but should inform him of the limits on confidentiality.

Psychologists should let employees using their company's employee assistance program (EAP) know that they will not release any confidential information to the employees' supervisors without the employees' authorization to do so.

Before deciding how to proceed, an ethical psychologist should consider whether their shared church membership with new clients is likely to impact their effectiveness as a therapist, in accordance with ethical standards prohibiting multiple relationships that could impair objectivity or competence.

Dr. Crosby, a licensed psychologist, should give her clients the phone number of a colleague who is willing to accept their calls and see them in case of an emergency during her two-week absence from her full-time private practice to spend time with her father having hip replacement surgery.

Dr. Watson, a newly licensed psychologist, is allowed to consult with a more experienced colleague about a new client without obtaining the client's authorization as long as he can disguise the client's identity, which is consistent with the APA Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
This practice is unethical since the intern should be identified as the person who administered and scored the tests.

A psychologist should tell the client that they cannot see the client's best friend in therapy and offer to give the friend referrals to other mental health professionals, as seeing the best friend would constitute an unacceptable multiple relationship.

Psychologists should usually avoid accepting contingent fees when acting as an expert witness in a legal case, as this is most consistent with the ethical requirements outlined in the APA's Ethics Code and Specialty Guidelines for Forensic Psychology, as well as the Canadian Code of Ethics.
Informed consents may be written or verbal but should be documented, as per the requirements of the ethics codes published by the American and Canadian Psychological Associations.

To be consistent with ethical guidelines, a psychologist conducting research with psychiatric inpatients who have legal guardians should obtain assent from each patient and informed consent from each patient's legal guardian.

To be consistent with ethical guidelines, Dr. Moore should refuse to provide Ms. Kazinsky's mother with information in Max's record without permission of the executor or administrator of his estate, as Max, a former client of Dr. Moore's, passed away two months ago at the age of 32.
Implied consent is inferred from the behaviors or circumstances of a person.

The primary concern with using Skype to provide psychotherapy on the Internet is the issue of confidentiality, as people may not be aware that their sessions could be recorded and released by the parent company.

A client who you stopped seeing in therapy two months ago calls you to request that you send her a summary of her assessment results by email, which you should do if she has been informed of the potential limits on confidentiality and the information in the email is encrypted.
The best course of action is to discuss with Jamie the need to share information about her binging and purging with her parents before contacting them.

A psychologist who has unknowingly become involved in a potentially harmful multiple relationship with a current therapy client and a relative of the client should seek consultation to help determine the best course of action, as required by ethical standards.

Psychologists do not have to obtain a client's authorization before discussing the client's case with a consultant if they can disguise the client's identity while doing so, according to the ethical guidelines of the American and Canadian Psychological Associations.

Dr. Hassan's decision to not provide therapy to Gerard G. due to her personal feelings regarding his past sexual assault conviction is acceptable if she provides him with referrals to other mental health professionals.

As an ethical psychologist, you will consider the nature of your therapeutic relationship with your client Maggie M. and the potential effect on her of your acceptance or refusal of her invitation to a party celebrating the completion of her dissertation before deciding whether or not to accept the invitation, in accordance with the APA's Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.

To be consistent with ethical requirements, you should send the school counselor only information you believe is relevant to your client Tyler's problems at school, as per the APA's Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.

When a 14-year-old client, Sally, says she has been thinking about killing herself, the best course of action is to continue discussing her feelings to determine if she is actually at risk for attempting suicide.

Under the Privacy Rule of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), a therapist can deny clients access to their protected health information when they believe that access is reasonably likely to endanger the life or physical safety of the client or other person.

The 1976 Tarasoff decision does not apply to the situation where a client discloses that he engaged in unsafe sex with three partners after receiving his HIV-positive test results 18 months ago but is no longer doing so, and the appropriate actions for the therapist and client depend on state or provincial laws.
A professional executor may be a licensed psychologist or other licensed health provider.

When reporting the results of your evaluation of a 35-year-old applicant for managerial positions at a national chain of toy stores, you do not include information about the applicant's abortion in your report.

Dr. Renee Rochester does not have to obtain informed consent from the defendant but should tell him about the nature of the services being provided and the limits of confidentiality when conducting a court-ordered evaluation of Terrance Tillis, the defendant in a criminal court case, to be consistent with the provisions of the APA's Specialty Guidelines for Forensic Psychology (2013).
When a forensic psychologist is hired to conduct a psychological evaluation of a defendant in a criminal case, the "client" is the person/entity that retained the psychologist.
A psychologist should refuse to conduct a child custody evaluation for a former therapy client, as this would constitute a multiple relationship.
Consumer Skype is not considered HIPAA compliant because it will not enter into a business associate agreement.

When a psychologist is providing therapy to an employee through an employee assistance program (EAP), the psychologist must not provide information to the employee's supervisor without authorization from the employee whether the employee's participation is the result of a self-referral or referral from the supervisor.

A psychologist providing individual therapy to inmates of an adult correctional facility should inform the appropriate prison official of an inmate's intent to physically harm another inmate, given the duty to protect and the priority of safety over confidentiality concerns.

When confidential information is faxed or otherwise transferred electronically, it is not possible to guarantee it will not be accessed by unauthorized individuals, so the best course of action is to remove all identifying information before faxing the requested information to the therapist.
A psychologist may refuse to forward a client's record to a colleague for nonpayment of fees only if the records are not needed for the client's emergency treatment.

Accepting contingent fees should usually be avoided, as the APA Ethics Code and Specialty Guidelines for Forensic Psychology state that the threat to impartiality presented by the acceptance of contingent fees should lead forensic practitioners to strive to avoid providing professional services on the basis of contingent fees.

Inviting Annie's husband to participate in Annie's therapy sessions for her social phobia is acceptable since the psychologist believes his participation will benefit Annie, as it is consistent with the standard that prohibits uninvited solicitation but allows attempting to implement appropriate collateral contacts for the purpose of benefiting an already engaged therapy client.
Agreeing to the arrangement where Mrs. Giovanni exchanges home cleaning services for therapy would be unethical, as it creates a potentially harmful multiple relationship.
This arrangement is unacceptable because psychologists are prohibited from compensating employees of newspapers in exchange for a newspaper article about their services.
To be consistent with ethical requirements, psychologists can solicit testimonials from former (but not current) clients as long as they're not vulnerable to undue influence.

APA's Record Keeping Guidelines recommend retaining the full client record until 7 years after the last date of service delivery for adults or until 3 years after a minor reaches the age of majority, whichever is later.
It is acceptable for psychologists to receive a fee from referral of clients to another psychologist only if the fee represents the psychologists' actual costs for referring the clients.

proprietary.content: Routinely waiving insurance co-payments without the insurance company's agreement constitutes insurance fraud and is unethical and illegal.
As an ethical psychologist, you should discuss the client's concerns and tell her that you need to keep a record of her sessions and explain your reasons for doing so.

To be consistent with ethical requirements, a psychologist will notify the client that they will contact a collection agency if the client does not pay for their services as agreed and does not respond to the psychologist's letters asking them to contact the psychologist to discuss the unpaid bill.

Using a collection agency to collect unpaid fees is acceptable only if the psychologist notifies the client of their intent and provides the client an opportunity to make prompt payment before doing so.
The designation "Ph.D. (Cand.)" is unacceptable even if it accurately identifies a graduate student's status, as it violates ethical standards by implying an earned credential.
Bartering may be acceptable according to the ethics codes of the American and Canadian Psychological Associations when it is not clinically contraindicated.
As an ethical psychologist, in-person solicitation of business may be acceptable if it is uninvited as long as it does not target people who are vulnerable to undue influence.

Unless a psychologist clearly communicates that responding to viewer emails and calls does not establish a therapeutic relationship, accepting an offer to present mental health information on a TV program would be unethical.
Psychologists can ethically place paid advertisements in newspapers as long as the columns are clearly identified as such.
Billing insurance companies for missed appointments without their approval would be insurance fraud, which is both unethical and illegal.

It is unacceptable for Dr. Lansky to list her Ph.D. in business administration on her business card and advertisements for her clinical psychology practice, as it does not meet the requirements of the APA's Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.
Psychologists should reach an agreement with new clients about fees and other financial issues as early as is feasible in the professional relationship.
A psychologist starting a private practice may offer the first therapy session for free to new clients if she clearly specifies her usual hourly fee and the purpose of the first session.

This situation is directly addressed in Standard 5.04 of the APA Ethics Code and indirectly addressed in Standard III.5 of the Canadian Code of Ethics, where the psychologist would want to make sure that callers understand that a professional therapeutic relationship is not established when she responds to their questions and that the advice or opinions she provides do not constitute therapy.
Withholding a client's record for nonpayment of fees is always unethical when the record is needed for the client's emergency treatment.
Billing an insurance company for a reimbursable form of therapy instead of the non-reimbursable form that's actually being provided is unethical.

Bartering therapy services for yard work and home repairs is unethical according to ethical guidelines, as the therapist would be acting as both therapist and employer, which could affect their objectivity and the therapeutic relationship.

A tort is a civil wrongdoing that results from a negligent breach of duty that results in injury or harm to a patient. Torts can be intentional or unintentional. Conversion (theft of or damage to personal property), infliction of emotional distress, and fraud/deceit are types of intentional torts. Unintentional torts (e.g., malpractice) involve negligence and are also known as negligence torts. Being familiar with the four conditions required for a claim of malpractice would have helped you identify the correct answer to this question: (a) The psychologist must have had a professional relationship with the patient that established the psychologist's duty to conform to a professional standard of care. (b) There was a breach of the duty (i.e., negligence) on the part of the psychologist. (c) The patient suffered injury or harm as a result of this breach. (d) The psychologist's breach of duty was the direct or proximate cause of the patient's harm or injury.
Withholding a therapy client's record for nonpayment of fees is always unethical when it's needed for the client's emergency treatment.
Psychologists must not engage in uninvited in-person solicitation of business from current or potential therapy clients or others who are vulnerable to undue influence.
Psychologists are prohibited from soliciting testimonials from current clients and, in some circumstances, former clients.

The 7th edition of the Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association states that authors should retain raw data associated with their articles published in APA journals in accordance with institutional or funder requirements.

Listing the University of Illinois on Dr. Jackson's business card for her clinical practice is not acceptable since her affiliation with the University of Illinois is not relevant to her clinical practice.

in_book.content: Informed consents are not necessary when the study involves investigating normal educational practices, as this is consistent with the provisions of the APA's Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.

proprietary.content: Psychologists are prohibited from becoming sexually involved with students over whom they have or are likely to have evaluative authority.

Changing the format of the presentation from a "lecture" to having attendees describe their personal experiences with eating disorders is unethical because it violates the requirements of the APA Ethics Code and Canadian Code of Ethics, which require psychologists to provide accurate descriptions of the content of the programs they provide.

Psychologists must allow research participants, who are students receiving class credit, to withdraw from a study at any time during the study, as required by the APA Ethics Code and Canadian Code of Ethics.

Dr. Oliver's requirement for students in his Psychology 101 class to participate in another professor's research project is acceptable only if students are given the choice of participating or completing an alternative assignment.

According to the ethical requirements for authorship of a journal article based substantially on a student's doctoral dissertation, the student must be listed as the principal author, except under exceptional circumstances.
Use of deception in research may be acceptable when alternative procedures are not available and subjects are informed about the deception "as early as is feasible."
Dr. Merritt's evaluation of Alice is not acceptable because it was not based entirely on Alice's actual performance as an intern.

A graduate program in clinical psychology requires first-year students to participate in individual therapy, which is acceptable as long as there are no multiple relationships between the students and the therapists according to the APA Ethics Code and the Canadian Code of Ethics.

Debriefing research participants about the nature and results of a research study is required, but in some cases, debriefing may not be necessary if scientific or humane values justify delaying or withholding this information.
Offering inducements to research participants, such as a gift card to a local restaurant, is acceptable as long as it is not likely to coerce participation.

It would be unacceptable for the post-doctoral student to list one of the professors in her department as the principal author of the article on the research study she has just completed, as the professor's contribution was relatively minor.
Authors of research articles published in APA journals must retain their data for at least 5 years after the date of publication.

According to the ethics codes published by the American and Canadian Psychological Associations, a psychologist who discovers an error in the description of the results of their statistical analysis in a published article is required to take action to correct the error.

In his dissertation proposal, a graduate student used the organization and headings used by the author of a published journal article, and used arguments and data presented by that author and the author of another published article on the same topic to justify his study's hypotheses, but he cited both authors only once in the introductory paragraph, which is unacceptable since the graduate student has not given adequate credit to the other authors.

Covering only research on aging that produces results similar to one's own studies in an introductory neuropsychology class would be unacceptable, as it violates ethical requirements to present instructional information in an accurate and unbiased manner.

The APA Ethics Code and Canadian Code of Ethics require psychologists to allow research participants to withdraw from a study at any time, so an ethical psychologist would allow the students to withdraw from the study.
Sexual relationships with supervisees over whom psychologists have evaluative authority are prohibited according to the ethics codes of the American and Canadian Psychological Associations.

This issue is addressed in Standard 7.04 of the APA's Ethics Code and the Values Statement for Standard I and Standard I.8 of the Canadian Code of Ethics. Standard 7.04 states that students should not be required to disclose personal information in course- or program-related activities related to psychological treatment except in two circumstances: (a) this requirement has been clearly identified in program and admissions materials or (b) the information is needed to "evaluate or obtain assistance for students whose personal problems could reasonably be judged to be preventing them from performing their training- or professionally related activities in a competent manner or posing a threat to the student or others."
This is acceptable as long as the client's complaint is valid and Dr. Devlin has previously provided the intern with feedback about his performance.
Psychologists may use deception in a research study when it's justified by the study's prospective value and participants are allowed to withdraw from the study at any time.
Psychologists may use animal subjects in research that causes them pain or stress when alternative procedures are unavailable and doing so is justified by the study's prospective value.

If a psychologist's former intern is not likely to be under the psychologist's evaluative authority in the future, a sexual relationship between them is considered acceptable according to ethical guidelines.

If Dr. Wendy Wundt terminates Lloyd's internship due to his recent behaviors, she will have acted ethically only if she first provides Lloyd with a plan to remediate his unacceptable behaviors and Lloyd continues to engage in those behaviors.
Offering monetary or other inducements to encourage people to volunteer for a research study is unacceptable if they're likely to coerce participation.
Dr. Morten and Dr. Chang are both responsible for the appropriate treatment of animal subjects in the rhesus monkey attachment research.

If a research psychologist decides it's not possible to conduct a study without deceiving participants about the true purpose, they must tell participants about the true purpose as early as feasible and allow them to withdraw their data.

The supervisor should determine if it's necessary to reassign the intern's current client to another therapist and discuss with the intern ways that might help her reconcile the conflict between her religious beliefs and the requirement that psychologists work effectively with diverse (including homosexual) clients.
Deception is never acceptable when a research study's procedures may cause participants physical pain or severe emotional distress.
Sexual relationships with students over whom psychologists have evaluative authority are prohibited according to the ethics codes of the American and Canadian Psychological Associations.
Psychologists should ordinarily debrief research participants immediately after their participation but, when that isn't possible, should take steps to reduce the risk for harm.
Except under exceptional circumstances, the student should be listed as principal author on any multiple-authored article that is substantially based on the student's doctoral dissertation.
Requiring psychology students to participate in individual or group therapy may be acceptable if they are allowed to select providers from mental health professionals not affiliated with the program.

Simultaneous (concurrent) submission of an article to multiple journals is unacceptable, as the author(s) should submit the article to one journal at a time and wait for it to be rejected by one journal before submitting it to another journal.

Psychologists may use animal subjects in research that may cause the animals pain or stress when alternative nonpainful and nonstressful procedures are unavailable and use of animals is justified by the potential value of the research.
Changing course requirements is acceptable for a psychology professor if the changes do not affect the ability of students to fulfill the new requirements by the end of the semester.

Before administering an intervention to children with bipolar disorder and acute stress disorder, the psychologist must obtain consent from the child's legal guardian(s) and assent from the child unless assent is waived on capacity grounds or grounds of direct benefit to the child.
A psychologist reviewing a research paper cannot use the unique ideas and procedures presented in the paper in their own research without first obtaining permission from the paper's authors.

in_book.content: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have a better tolerability profile than the tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) and greater safety in overdose.

The best course of action for a young man with schizophrenia who develops tardive dyskinesia while taking a conventional antipsychotic is to replace the conventional antipsychotic with an atypical antipsychotic.

The tertiary amines (e.g., amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine) exert their effects by inhibiting the reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine, with some having a greater effect on serotonin, while the secondary amines (e.g., nortriptyline, desipramine) are more potent at inhibiting the reuptake of norepinephrine than serotonin.

When a patient with schizophrenia is taking a neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drug and develops the symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, the drug should be discontinued immediately because it is a life-threatening side effect.

An older adult taking a conventional antipsychotic is at the greatest risk for developing tardive dyskinesia, a condition involving repetitive involuntary movements caused by long-term use of antipsychotic drugs.
A person taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) should avoid eating foods containing tyramine.

Of the antipsychotics, the atypical drug clozapine is most likely to produce agranulocytosis, a rare but potentially fatal blood disorder characterized by an abnormally low level of white blood cells, requiring regular blood monitoring.
The risk for developing agranulocytosis, a potentially fatal blood disorder, is greatest for the antipsychotic drug clozapine.
The risk for tardive dyskinesia is greatest for a 70-year-old woman taking an antipsychotic drug as a treatment for schizophrenia.
SSRIs and SNRIs are both considered first-line pharmacological treatments for major depressive disorder.

Combining an SSRI with an MAOI, lithium, or other serotonergic drug can cause serotonin syndrome, and treatment involves immediate withdrawal of the serotonergic drugs and providing appropriate medical interventions for the patient's symptoms.
Risperidone and other second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic drugs are serotonin and dopamine antagonists.
A hypertensive crisis may occur when foods containing tyramine are consumed while taking the drug phenelzine.
Akathisia is a movement disorder caused by antipsychotic drugs and is characterized by a sense of restlessness and an urge to keep moving.
Clozapine and, to a lesser extent, other SGAs can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis, which is a severe form of neutropenia.

If a person with bipolar I disorder is not taking a mood stabilizing drug but begins taking an SSRI to treat her current depressive symptoms, the SSRI may trigger rapid cycling or manic symptoms, as treating the depression of bipolar I disorder with an SSRI or other antidepressant can trigger mania or hypomania or rapid cycling, and treatment guidelines generally recommend prescribing an antidepressant for individuals with bipolar I disorder only when the person is also taking a mood stabilizer.
Anticonvulsant drugs, such as carbamazepine, are often prescribed for individuals with bipolar disorder who have not responded to lithium or cannot tolerate its side effects.
Lithium is used to treat bipolar disorder.
Memantine, unlike galantamine, rivastigmine, and donepezil, does not slow the cognitive decline caused by Alzheimer's disease by increasing cholinergic activity.

Propranolol and atenolol have been found useful for relieving the physical symptoms of some types of anxiety (especially performance-related anxiety), but they do not have a direct effect on its emotional or cognitive symptoms.
Disulfiram (Antabuse) causes nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, and other unpleasant symptoms when taken in conjunction with alcohol.
Naltrexone reduces the rewarding effects of alcohol and cravings for alcohol for a middle-aged patient who has just received a diagnosis of alcohol use disorder.
Benzodiazepines with a shorter half-life are preferred for older adults, and tapering should be slow to reduce the risk and severity of withdrawal symptoms.

The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative measure of the relative safety of a drug that is calculated by dividing the lethal dose 50 (LD50), which indicates the minimum drug dose that had a lethal effect in 50% of a test sample, by the effective dose 50 (ED50), which indicates the minimum drug dose that produced the therapeutic (desired) effect in 50% of a test sample, with a larger TI indicating a safer drug.
GABA agonists, such as benzodiazepines and barbiturates, produce relaxation and sleepiness.
Carbamazepine and valproic acid are anticonvulsant drugs that are considered alternatives to lithium as first-line treatments for the manic episodes associated with bipolar disorder.
For college students without ADHD, taking methylphenidate and other stimulant drugs has positive effects on attention and mood but no beneficial effects on GPA.
Diazepam, alprazolam, and lorazepam are benzodiazepines that are used to treat anxiety and insomnia.
Based on Mr. Wolf's symptoms characteristic of Parkinson's disease, the most effective pharmacological treatment for him is likely to be levodopa.
Dronabinol is a synthetic form of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) that has been FDA approved for the treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
The hallucinogenic drug lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) is a serotonin agonist.
The effects of methylphenidate, nicotine, cocaine, and other psychostimulants are mediated primarily by the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine.
THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), the main psychoactive chemical in marijuana, produces its reinforcing effects by increasing dopamine concentrations in the nucleus accumbens.
Venlafaxine and duloxetine are SNRIs that are used to treat major depressive disorder, social anxiety disorder, and neuropathic pain.
When symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) do not respond adequately to SSRIs or SNRIs, the drug-of-choice is often the anxiolytic buspirone (Buspar) or a benzodiazepine.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) has been linked to low levels of serotonin.
St. John's wort should not be taken with an SSRI because doing so can cause serotonin syndrome.

Research has found that electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) has the fastest time to remission of symptoms compared to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), interpersonal therapy (IPT), and antidepressant drugs as treatments for severe depression.
St. John's wort extract is not significantly different from SSRIs in terms of treatment response for mild to moderate depression and has a lower rate of adverse events.

Esketamine, a nasal spray version of ketamine, has been found to be an effective treatment for treatment-resistant depression.

in_book.content: The nonpharmacological treatment-of-choice for insomnia disorder is a multi-component cognitive-behavioral intervention that incorporates stimulus control or sleep restriction with sleep-hygiene education, relaxation training, and/or cognitive therapy.
The medication most useful for reducing daytime sleepiness, improving nighttime sleep, and reducing cataplexy in narcolepsy is sodium oxybate.
Antipsychotic drugs that reduce dopamine activity in certain areas of the brain have been found useful for suppressing tics.
Autism spectrum disorder has been linked to low brain level and high blood level of serotonin.

The research is not entirely consistent with regard to the association between the use of stimulant drugs by children with ADHD and risk for developing an SUD later in life, with a meta-analysis finding that the use of stimulant medications to treat children with ADHD neither increased nor decreased the risk for later development of an SUD, but a more recent study finding that children with ADHD who began treatment with a stimulant drug at a young age and at a high dose were less likely to develop an SUD than were those who began treatment at an older age and at a lower dose.
Clozapine is considered the most effective medication for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
Drugs that increase serotonin are often used to treat premature ejaculation.

proprietary.content: Paroxetine is an alternative to behavioral treatments for premature ejaculation.

in_book.content: Research on smoking cessation interventions suggests that counseling and medication are each effective when used alone but the combination of counseling and medication is most effective.
The studies have not yet identified a pharmacological treatment that is consistently effective for cocaine addiction (substance use disorder in the DSM-5).
